# spine: does closing a branch save the money the study projects, or move the cost somewhere the study does not count?
[S1] Start with Eastlin, because everything else in the study is measured against it. The branch closed in June of twenty twenty-two. Sixteen hundred active cardholders, sixteen thousand items circulated in its last full year.
[S2] And the projection was three hundred ten thousand dollars a year saved. The study confirms the money came off the books. So on the only test anybody applied at the time, the closure worked.
[S1] Then somebody kept counting. The system tracked those sixteen hundred cards for the year after the doors shut. Circulation by those cardholders fell forty-four percent, and only twenty-nine percent registered at another branch.
[S2] Which tells you the savings were real and the assumption underneath them failed. The projection assumed displaced readers turn up somewhere else in the system. Most of them did not turn up anywhere.
[S1] Aurelio Pinter writes that the Eastlin result is the most important number in the report and the one the board has never been shown. That is a consultant naming the thing that hurts.
[S2] Okay. Set the table for me, because I want to know how big this system is before we start closing pieces of it, and who asked for the study.
[S1] Calder Valley runs fourteen branches across eleven towns for two hundred fourteen thousand people. Marisol Deeb chairs the board, commissioned the work in September of twenty twenty-five, and had it in hand by July.
[S2] Deeb also set one condition worth keeping in view. Every closure the study proposes has to arrive with at least one costed alternative beside it. That condition does real work at the end.
[S1] Circulation first. One million four hundred thousand items in fiscal twenty nineteen, one million one hundred twenty thousand in fiscal twenty twenty-six. Twenty percent down across the seven years the study covers.
[S2] The headline hides a split, though. Physical circulation fell thirty-one percent. Digital rose eighty-four percent, from fourteen percent of the total to thirty-eight percent. Two different systems living inside one number.
[S1] Here is where I complicate my own thread. The collections budget fell from one million nine hundred thousand dollars to one million four hundred eighty thousand today. That is twenty-two percent less to buy with.
[S2] And new physical items dropped from thirty-eight thousand a year to twenty-one thousand a year. Forty-five percent fewer new books reaching the shelves. A system buying less will circulate less.
[S1] Pinter draws the consequence for the closure question. A small branch with a thin new-materials shelf posts a circulation decline that reads as a demand problem and is partly a purchasing decision made upstream.
[S2] Which matters, because the screen for closure is built on circulation. Under fifteen thousand items a year, or cost per item over double the system average of sixteen dollars, or deferred maintenance past a quarter of assessed value.
[S1] Four branches tripped at least one condition. Gullick, Dunmoor, Bell Quarry, and Norbeck. Gullick is the extreme case, and every other number in the review gets read against it.
[S2] Give me Gullick, then. I have already seen the cost line quoted in the summary, and I want the building before anybody hands me the dollars per item.
[S1] Built in nineteen thirty-one as a grange hall, handed to the town in nineteen sixty-eight. Twenty-two hundred square feet. Open eighteen hours a week across three days. It circulated nine thousand four hundred items.
[S2] Five hundred seventy thousand dollars a year to run that. Sixty-one dollars per circulated item, against a system average of sixteen. Close to four times over. That is the number on the slide.
[S1] With one million three hundred thousand dollars of deferred maintenance sitting on it. Most of that is a roof replacement and a boiler the facilities report calls past its service life and still running.
[S2] Tomas Vry manages the branch and answered the draft in writing. First point. Eighteen hours is the fewest in the system, and circulation per open hour at Gullick beats Munce Road, which is open thirty-two.
[S1] The second point is the sharper one. That one million three hundred thousand dollar maintenance figure assumes the building stays a library. The town has asked twice about taking the building back.
[S2] So the backlog number and the closure number are the same roof counted twice... and if the town takes the building, the roof becomes the town's problem and the savings line does not move.
[S1] Dunmoor next. Twelve thousand items, three hundred eighty thousand dollars a year, thirty-two dollars an item. The building was renovated in twenty fifteen, so it fails on circulation and passes on facilities.
[S2] Dunmoor is the distance case. Harrow Mill is fourteen miles away, the bus runs four times a day and takes fifty-two minutes, and forty-one percent of Dunmoor's surveyed users arrived on foot or by bus.
[S1] The study says plainly that it has no measure of how many of those users would reach Harrow Mill. Sitting next to the Eastlin tracking, that silence reads as an answer.
[S2] Bell Quarry is the one that made me trust Pinter more. Forty-one thousand items circulated, forty-six hours open, twenty-nine dollars an item. The screen caught it purely on cost per item.
[S1] Then look at the program calendar. Eleven thousand people attended programs at Bell Quarry in fiscal twenty twenty-six, eighteen percent of the system total. It is the busiest building Calder Valley operates.
[S2] So Pinter pulls it off the list and says the screen was wrong. Count circulation and Bell Quarry looks expensive. Count the people through the door and it is the flagship.
[S1] Norbeck comes off the list on arithmetic alone. The lease runs to twenty thirty-one with no early termination, so closing the branch saves the staffing cost and none of the occupancy cost.
[S2] And the survey adds the part that would have made the closure a story. Seventy-three percent of Norbeck users reported no home broadband, and fifty-eight percent of visits there were for the public computers.
[S1] Which leaves Gullick and Dunmoor. Their combined operating cost is nine hundred fifty thousand dollars. The study calls six hundred forty thousand of that genuinely avoidable, and the remainder follows the collections wherever they land.
[S2] Then take the staff back out. Forty-seven percent of that six hundred forty thousand is staff the board would reassign rather than lay off. Net annual saving, three hundred forty thousand dollars.
[S1] Against an operating budget of eighteen million. The study writes the ratio out rather than leaving it for a reader to find. The two closures save under two percent of the budget.
[S2] And one hundred twenty thousand dollars of that goes once to moving and absorbing the two collections. So the first year nets close to nothing, and two towns lose their library building.
[S1] The backlog is the other frame the board will hear. Twenty-four million dollars of deferred maintenance across fourteen buildings, with six buildings carrying seventy-eight percent of it. Gullick takes one million three hundred thousand off.
[S2] Removing a number from a backlog does not fund the rest of it. The study says that about itself, then recommends a capital plan before any closure vote. That recommendation is the honest one.
[S1] Staffing is thinner than the buildings are. Two hundred fourteen people in fiscal twenty nineteen, one hundred eighty-seven now. Twenty-seven F T E positions gone, and a vacancy rate of twelve percent in June.
[S2] Plus eighteen thousand hours of substitute coverage bought to keep the advertised hours open. Okonjo's memo argues a closure now would read to staff as ratifying the vacancies. Pinter does not answer that.
[S1] The peer comparison surprised me. Pell Lundgren set Calder Valley against three similar systems, and their circulation declines over the same seven years ran seventeen percent, twenty-three percent, and twenty-nine percent.
[S2] So the decline is not a local management failure. One of those peers closed a branch and tracked the displaced cardholders. Their circulation fell thirty-eight percent, against the forty-four percent after Eastlin.
[S1] Two independent measurements landing that close is the strongest evidence in the report. Pinter says so, and then says two observations are not a trend, which is the right amount of caution.
[S2] Then the alternatives Deeb insisted on. Cutting four open hours a week at all fourteen branches saves four hundred ten thousand dollars a year, more than the two closures net after reassignment.
[S1] A bookmobile costs two hundred eighty thousand a year, and nobody can say what it would circulate, since the system has never run one. Merging technical services saves one hundred ninety thousand.
[S2] And the question none of it touches is the levy formula, which Deeb ruled out of scope at the start. Pinter notes the exclusion and says it is what every speaker was actually asking.
[S1] Eleven hearings, three hundred forty speakers, sixty-two percent opposed to any closure at all. Hattie Bream of Norbeck gets the line the study quotes and leaves alone: which numbers did the board agree to count?
[S2] So here is where I land. The money is real and it is small. The cost that is large is the one Eastlin measured and nobody budgeted for, and both now sit on one page.
[S1] Same place, from the other end. I would close Gullick if the town takes the building back, and count the cardholders afterward. The only reason we know what a closure costs is that somebody counted once.
